title: An extraordinary celestial spiral around LL Pegasi
caption: The spiral around LL Pegasi, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: LL Pegasi, AFGL 3068, IRAS 23166+1655 · constellation Pegasus

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A near-perfect spiral winds outward from a hidden star in this Hubble image, as regular as a groove on a record. The star is LL Pegasi, in Pegasus, and the spiral is the very beginning of a planetary nebula, cataloged as IRAS 23166+1655. Thick dust still hides the star at its center.

The pattern is thought to come from a pair of stars. One is shedding gas as it ages while it circles a companion, so each orbit lays down another turn of the spiral. Astronomers estimate the shells are about 800 years apart, matching the estimated time the two stars take to orbit each other.

Stars from about half the Sun's mass up to around eight times it don't end as supernovae. They puff off their outer layers instead, building the delicate shapes we see as planetary nebulae. LL Pegasi is only starting down that road, with its gas streaming out at about 50,000 kilometers per hour.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys combined a yellow-visible filter, shown in blue, and a near-infrared filter, shown in red, with a green channel made from both.
understand.eye: The spiral shines by reflected starlight in dust, far too faint for the eye; the colors are a two-filter rendering, not natural hues.

explore: The image combines exposures of 11 minutes through the yellow filter and 22 minutes through the near-infrared one, and spans about 80 arcseconds of sky.
alt: A faint, regular spiral of dust coiling outward from a hidden central star.
